As a React developer, I’ve encountered the term rendering many times while working on different projects. I wanted to take a deeper dive into this concept to strengthen my understanding of how React works under the hood.
What is Rendering?
In web development, rendering is the process of converting code into visual, interactive content that users can see and interact with in their browsers.
Simply put, rendering is the process of transforming written code into a functional user interface.
Over the years, modern frameworks have introduced many new rendering strategies and concepts, such as CSR (Client-Side Rendering), SSR (Server-Side Rendering), SSG (Static Site Generation), ISG (Incremental Static Generation), and resumability. As web technologies continue to evolve, even more rendering approaches are likely to emerge.

Why is DOM Manipulation Expensive?
The Document Object Model (DOM) is a programming interface for web documents. It represents an HTML or XML document as a tree of objects that JavaScript can read and manipulate.
A Virtual DOM (VDOM) is a lightweight, in-memory representation of the real DOM. Frameworks like React use the Virtual DOM to optimize UI updates and minimize expensive DOM manipulations.
The Virtual DOM keeps an ideal representation of the UI in memory. Whenever the application state changes, React creates a new Virtual DOM tree and compares it with the previous one. This comparison process is called reconciliation.
Directly manipulating the real DOM is expensive because every modification may trigger browser work such as recalculating layouts, repainting elements, and updating the rendered page. Even a small change can have a cascading effect across the DOM tree.

What Problem Does React Solve?
React solves the challenge of building and maintaining complex user interfaces in a predictable and efficient way.
Although it’s possible to manipulate the DOM directly using JavaScript or jQuery, managing large and dynamic applications quickly becomes difficult. React simplifies this by introducing a Virtual DOM, a component-based architecture, and a declarative programming model.
React efficiently updates only the parts of the UI that have changed by comparing the previous and current Virtual DOM trees. It also provides state and props, making data flow predictable and UI updates easier to reason about.

What Triggers a Render in React?
A React component re-renders when one of the following occurs:

• Its state changes.

• Its props change.

• Its parent component re-renders.

• A subscribed context value changes.

• A render is explicitly triggered (for example, using forceUpdate() in class components).
When setState (or a state setter returned by useState) is called, React doesn't immediately update the DOM. Instead, it queues the state update and schedules a new render.
During the render process, React compares the newly generated Virtual DOM with the previous one. If differences are found, React updates only the affected parts of the real DOM.

React’s Rendering Lifecycle
1. State Update Phase

• React queues state updates.

• React schedules a render for the affected component.
2. Render Phase

• React calls your component with the latest state and props.

• Your component returns new JSX.

• React creates a new Virtual DOM tree.
3. Reconciliation Phase

• React compares the new Virtual DOM with the previous one.

• It determines exactly which elements have changed.
4. Commit Phase

• React applies the minimum required changes to the real DOM.

• Browser painting occurs.

• useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutations.

• useEffect runs asynchronously after the browser has painted the UI.
5. Cleanup Phase
When a component is unmounted or an effect is about to re-run, React executes the cleanup functions returned from useEffect.

Summary
React rendering is more than simply updating the DOM. It follows a carefully designed pipeline:

• Queue state updates.

• Render a new Virtual DOM.

• Reconcile the old and new trees.

• Commit the minimal DOM changes.

• Execute effects and cleanup when necessary.
This architecture allows React to efficiently update the UI while minimizing expensive DOM operations, making it well suited for building complex, interactive applications.
